summary: Noah prays because evil spirits afflict his descendants; most are bound, a tenth remain under Mastêmâ, and angels teach Noah remedies he records for Shem. After Noah's death the narrative turns to the tower at Babel, the scattering of languages, Canaan's settlement in land outside his lot, and Madai's different request for land.
whyItMatters: The chapter explains why evil persists after the flood and shows the earlier land oath becoming consequential after Babel's dispersion.

context.author: Within the book, the angel of the presence dictates the account to Moses; the historical writer is unnamed.
context.audience: Israel is addressed through Moses in the book’s frame; the specific first historical audience is not identified.
context.date: The narrative places the revelation at Sinai; the historical Hebrew work is usually dated to the second century BCE, without an established exact year.
context.setting: From Noah's later lifetime through the Babel settlement and the movements of his descendants.
context.literaryForm: Angelic conflict and prayer followed by chronology, Babel narrative, and territorial explanation.

before.text: Noah’s descendants have sworn to respect their separate territorial lots.

here.text: The chapter explains post-flood spirits, Babel’s dispersal, and Canaan’s breach of the allotment.

after.text: The story turns toward Abraham’s ancestors, beginning with generations and the persistence of corrupt worship.

outline.heading: Noah prays over afflicted descendants
outline.note: He asks for the spirits associated with the Watchers to be restrained.

outline.heading: Most spirits bound; Noah receives remedies
outline.note: Mastêmâ retains a tenth while Noah writes and gives knowledge to Shem.

outline.heading: Noah’s death and the tower’s construction
outline.note: The genealogy and Babel building follow his burial.

outline.heading: Languages confused and builders dispersed
outline.note: God interrupts the project and the tower is overthrown.

outline.heading: Canaan and Madai choose their lands
outline.note: Canaan ignores a boundary warning; Madai obtains a share by request.

keyVerses.text: And He said: Let the tenth part of them remain before him, and let nine parts descend into the place of condemnation.'
keyVerses.why: The one-tenth decision is the chapter's explicit explanation for why some hostile spirits remain active.

keyVerses.text: And he confounded their language, and they no longer understood one another's speech, and they ceased then to build the city and the tower.
keyVerses.why: The confusion of language ends the common building effort and leads to the dispersion.

questions.question: What trouble brings Noah’s sons to him?
questions.answer: They say unclean demons are misleading, blinding, and killing their children. Noah responds with prayer for protection rather than a description of an ordinary illness alone.

questions.question: Who is Mastêmâ in this chapter?
questions.answer: He is called the chief of the spirits and asks that some remain under his authority. The narration later also calls him Satan; these verses describe his request and the permitted tenth without offering a full biography.

questions.question: Why are any hostile spirits left on earth?
questions.answer: Mastêmâ argues that he needs some for his work of leading people astray, and God permits a tenth while nine parts are bound. The passage states the decision but does not explain every theological reason behind that permission.

questions.question: Why does Noah write a book of medicines?
questions.answer: The angels teach him remedies and how to address the spirits’ seductions, and he records the instruction for Shem. The text presents both healing and written transmission as a response to continuing post-flood danger.

questions.question: What does “Babel” explain in this story?
questions.answer: The narrator links the name with God’s confounding of a once-shared language. Once the builders cannot understand one another, they stop work and disperse into distinct cities and nations.

questions.question: Are the tower’s exact dimensions a measurement readers can verify today?
questions.answer: This edition supplies large figures and units for the building, then says a wind overthrew it. The ancient numbers belong to the narrated account; the chapter does not identify surviving remains that would let a reader verify those measurements.

questions.question: Why do Ham and his sons object to Canaan’s settlement?
questions.answer: They say the Lebanon region belongs to Shem’s share, while Canaan has a separate inheritance assigned by lot. Their warning applies the oath made before Noah in chapter 9, even though Canaan refuses to listen.

questions.question: How is Madai’s move different from Canaan’s?
questions.answer: Madai dislikes his original area and asks relatives for another portion, then settles near his wife’s brother. The chapter deliberately reports a request and agreement alongside Canaan’s refusal of a warning.

glossary.def: Hostile spirits said here to mislead and harm Noah’s descendants.
The name the narrator connects with the confounding of a shared human language.
